title: First Aid: Cuts, Scrapes, and Minor Burns
content:
Most minor cuts, scrapes, and burns can be treated safely at home. Knowing what to do — and what signs indicate a need for medical attention — helps prevent infection and supports healing.

For minor cuts and scrapes:
Apply direct pressure with a clean cloth or gauze for 5–10 minutes to stop bleeding. Do not remove the cloth if it becomes soaked; add more material on top. Once bleeding stops, rinse the wound gently under clean running water for several minutes to remove debris. Do not use hydrogen peroxide or iodine directly in the wound — these can damage tissue and slow healing. Apply a thin layer of antibiotic ointment (such as bacitracin) if available, then cover with a clean adhesive bandage. Change the dressing daily or when it becomes wet or dirty.

Seek medical attention for a cut if: it is longer than about 2 cm (about 3/4 inch) or the edges cannot be held together; it is deep enough to see yellow fatty tissue; it is on the face, hands, or genitals and may need stitches for cosmetic or functional reasons; it was caused by a dirty or rusty object (tetanus risk); the person has not had a tetanus shot in the last 5 years; or there are signs of infection (increasing redness, swelling, warmth, pus, or red streaks spreading from the wound).

For minor burns (first-degree: redness and pain; no blisters):
Cool the burn immediately with cool — not cold or ice — running water for 10–20 minutes. Cooling with ice or very cold water can cause further tissue damage. Do not apply butter, toothpaste, or oil — these trap heat and increase infection risk. After cooling, apply aloe vera gel or a mild moisturiser and loosely cover with a non-stick bandage.

Seek medical attention for burns that: are larger than about 7 cm (3 inches); involve the face, hands, feet, genitals, buttocks, or a major joint; appear white, brown, or black (possible second- or third-degree burn); or were caused by chemicals or electricity.
